faq.q: What's a genus?
faq.a: Every plant has a two-part Latin name, like *Opuntia microdasys*. The first word is the **genus**: a group of closely related plants, like a family name. The second word is the **species**, the specific plant, like a first name. So *Opuntia* is the genus of all prickly pears, and *microdasys* is the bunny ears cactus.

faq.q: How do reservations work?
faq.a: We can't bring every plant to every event, so browse the whole shop, reserve what you want, and choose the event you'll attend. We bring your plants there and message you to confirm. You pay in person when you pick them up.

faq.q: Do you ship?
faq.a: No. Plants are pickup only, at our farmers market and events. Check the [Upcoming events](index.html#events) section for where we'll be.

faq.q: Where can I find you?
faq.a: Every Saturday, 8am–12pm, at Roadrunner Park Farmers Market, [3502 E Cactus Rd, Phoenix, AZ 85032](https://www.google.com/maps/search/?api=1&query=3502+E+Cactus+Rd%2C+Phoenix%2C+AZ+85032) (opens a map). For other locations we update the site and post on social media a couple of days before.

faq.q: How do I pay?
faq.a: You pay when you pick up your plants at the event. There are no online payments.

faq.q: How often should I water my cactus?
faq.a: Water deeply, then wait until the soil is completely dry before watering again. In the Arizona summer that is usually every week or two, and in winter much less, often once a month or less. Use a pot with a drainage hole and never leave it sitting in water. Too much water hurts a cactus faster than too little.

faq.q: What if a plant is sold out?
faq.a: Sold out plants show a banner and can't be reserved. Join the email list at the bottom of the page and we'll send you a weekly update whenever we update the inventory.

faq.q: Can I reserve more than one of a plant?
faq.a: Yes, up to the number we have in stock, which is shown on each plant's page.

faq.q: How do I handle a prickly pear safely?
faq.a: Carry it by the pot. Opuntia pads have spines and tiny hair-like barbs called glochids that irritate skin. Use tongs or thick gloves if you need to touch the plant.

faq.q: Who do I contact with questions?
faq.a: Message [@azcactusdoctor](https://instagram.com/azcactusdoctor) or ask us at the market.

faq.q: What's the difference between a cactus and a succulent?
faq.a: Every cactus is a succulent, but not every succulent is a cactus. Succulents store water in thick leaves, stems or roots. Cacti are a family of succulents that have **areoles**, the small cushions where spines, flowers and new growth come from. Agave, Haworthia and Euphorbia are succulents that are not cacti.

faq.q: How much sun does a cactus need?
faq.a: Most cacti and succulents want bright light, and many need **6 or more hours of direct sun**. In Arizona, ease new plants into full sun over a week or two and give them afternoon shade in summer, because they can sunburn. A sunburned plant shows pale, tan or scarred patches that don't heal.

faq.q: Can I grow a cactus indoors?
faq.a: Yes, if you have a very bright spot, like a south or west window, or a grow light. Indoor plants grow more slowly and need less water than outdoor ones. If a plant stretches thin and pale toward the light, it needs more light.

faq.q: What is the best soil for cactus and succulents?
faq.a: A coarse, fast-draining cactus mix, ideally with extra pumice, perlite or coarse sand. Regular potting soil stays wet too long and can rot the roots. Always use a pot with a drainage hole.

faq.q: How do I know if I'm overwatering my cactus?
faq.a: Overwatering signs: a soft, mushy or blackened base, yellowing, or a plant that feels loose in the pot. Rot spreads fast, so let the soil dry completely between waterings and never leave the pot sitting in water. If the base is already soft, unpot the plant and cut away the rot.

faq.q: Why is my cactus wrinkled or shriveling?
faq.a: A wrinkled, soft or shriveled plant is usually thirsty. Water it deeply and it should plump up within days. If it wrinkles even with wet soil, the roots may be damaged by rot or pests, so check them.

faq.q: When should I repot a cactus?
faq.a: Repot when roots fill the pot or push out the drainage hole, usually every 2 to 3 years, in spring or summer. Pick a pot only slightly larger. Wear thick gloves or fold newspaper around spiny plants, and wait a week or so before watering so any damaged roots can heal.

faq.q: Does my cactus pot need a drainage hole?
faq.a: Yes. A drainage hole is the single best protection against root rot. If you love a pot without one, keep the cactus in a plain nursery pot and set it inside, and never let water collect in the bottom.

faq.q: Can cacti survive Arizona summers?
faq.a: Many can. Cacti and spiny desert plants are built for heat, but fleshy succulents and new plants can scorch in direct afternoon sun. Plants in pots get hotter than plants in the ground, so move pots to bright shade in the hottest months and water deeply less often, early in the morning.

faq.q: Can cacti survive a frost or freezing winter?
faq.a: It depends on the plant. Many hardy cacti, like prickly pear, handle brief light frosts when dry. Tender plants such as Adenium and many succulents can be damaged below about **50°F** and killed by a freeze. When a freeze is forecast, bring potted plants inside or cover them overnight, and keep them dry.

faq.q: What is a caudex plant?
faq.a: A caudex is a swollen, water-storing base or trunk, like the fat bottom of an Adenium or desert rose. Collectors love caudex plants for their sculptural shape. Keep the caudex above the soil line, give it fast-draining soil, and don't overwater it.

faq.q: How do I care for an Adenium (desert rose)?
faq.a: Give it a lot of sun (6 or more hours), a gritty fast-draining mix, and water only when the soil is dry. Feed in spring and summer, and keep it warm, above about 50°F. Adeniums are tropical, so they won't tolerate freezing. All parts are toxic, so keep them away from pets and kids.

faq.q: Why is my Adenium dropping its leaves?
faq.a: Often it's normal dormancy. Adeniums slow down and drop leaves in cool weather or short days. Water much less in winter. Leaf drop in warm weather can also mean too much or too little water, or a sudden move to lower light.

faq.q: How and when should I fertilize a cactus?
faq.a: Feed lightly in the growing season, spring through summer, with a diluted fertilizer made for cacti and succulents, a few times a year. Skip fertilizer in fall and winter and never feed a dry, stressed or newly repotted plant.

faq.q: How big do agaves get, and are they safe?
faq.a: It depends on the species. Some agaves stay small enough for a pot, and others grow into big, sharp-tipped rosettes. Plant them where you won't brush against the spined leaf tips, and give them room to reach their full size.

faq.q: Are cacti and succulents safe for kids and pets?
faq.a: Be careful. Spines hurt, Opuntia pads have tiny barbs called glochids, and Euphorbia has a milky sap that irritates skin and eyes. Adenium is toxic if eaten. Keep spiny and toxic plants out of reach of children and pets and wear gloves when handling them.

faq.q: How do I get rid of mealybugs and other pests on cactus?
faq.a: Mealybugs look like small cotton-like tufts. Dab them with rubbing alcohol on a cotton swab, or spray with insecticidal soap or neem oil, and repeat weekly until gone. Quarantine new plants and keep the plant in good light with dry soil, since pests like stressed plants.

faq.q: Why isn't my cactus blooming?
faq.a: Most cacti bloom only when mature, and they usually need strong sun, a cooler and drier winter rest, and the right amount of growing-season water. A plant kept in low light or watered year-round often won't flower. Some species just take years to reach blooming size.

faq.q: How do I propagate a cactus or succulent?
faq.a: Many cacti make pups or offsets that you can separate and root. Prickly pear pads can root after the cut end dries for a few days. Let any cut or cutting **callus for several days to a week** before planting in dry, gritty soil, and wait to water until roots form.

faq.q: Is it legal to dig up wild cactus in Arizona?
faq.a: No. Arizona protects many native desert plants, including the saguaro, and you generally need a permit and the landowner's permission to remove them. Buy nursery-grown plants from sellers like us instead, which also protects the desert.
